title: The Loom of the Republic
dek: On what American advertising must become, now that it has become the Nation's picture of itself
subject: Advertising's role in shaping American national vision
voice_note: Written in the voice of Thomas Carlyle (1795–1881), through the writer-carlyle skill. An emulation — the prose and judgments are not the historical Carlyle’s own words.
body:
We have, then, decided it: this Republic, once a Nation of Farmers, then a Nation of Workshops, is become, in these years of our Lord, a Nation of Advertisements. Turn it how you will, deny it who dares,— the plain arithmetic of the thing will not be argued down. More of the American's waking hour is spent under the persuading Voice than under any Pulpit, Parliament, or Schoolroom his Fathers built for him; more of the Republic's wealth is meted out to the men who make the Voice speak than to the men who dig the coal or lay the rail or teach the child his letters. Advertising is not, then, some decent adjunct trade, some mere upholstery clapped upon Commerce to help it sell its wares,— it is become, whether the Advertising Man knows it or no, the actual Loom on which the Nation's picture of itself is daily woven. Whoso sits at that Loom is not a Tradesman merely; he is, in the most fearful and literal sense, a Legislator; for what he weaves, thirty millions of eyes will look upon before they look upon anything else this day, and by that weaving will shape what they take to be desirable, possible, and true.

This being granted,— and it is granted the moment you count the dollars and the hours,— the question ceases to be, "How shall Advertising sell more soap?" and becomes the older and more terrible question that every Ruling Class of every Age has had put to it, whether it would or no: "What Vision hast thou for the People thou rulest?" For Rule it is. Adam Smith's invisible hand has, in our day, hired itself a very visible mouth, and that mouth talks to the Republic more hours in the year than any Statesman, and is trusted, alas, rather better. It is idle, therefore, to go on treating Madison Avenue and its innumerable digital heirs as though they were still peddling nostrums from a cart, some harmless Yankee huckstering to be regulated a little and then forgotten. No: the Huckster's cart has become the Nation's Pulpit, without anyone's quite resolving that it should; and now, resolved or not, there it stands, and thirty millions listen to it between their breakfast and their labor.

II.

Well, then,— thou Huckster-Elevated-to-Pulpit, thou Salesman suddenly finding a Sceptre in thy hand where thou didst expect only a sample-case,— what wilt thou do with it? For do something with it thou must; a Sceptre held is never neutral; it either builds a Cosmos or it lets the Chaos in, there is no third estate open to it. Here is the whole burden of what I have to say to thee, and I will say it plainly, in the plainest words this old tongue commands.

Thou shalt not, in the first place, go on pretending that thou art merely "moving product," as thy own Cant-phrase has it, while all the while thou art in very fact moving Desire itself,— manufacturing, in thy laboratories of persuasion, the very wants that yesterday did not exist and that tomorrow shall be spoken of by the People as needs older than their own birth. This is a godlike power, be it never so disguised in spreadsheets and click-through rates; and a godlike power exercised in a fit of absence of mind, without so much as asking what sort of Man it is making, is the very definition of that Mechanical Age I have elsewhere denounced,— the Age that builds engines of enormous force and appoints no one to ask what they are for.

If, then, thou wilt hold the Sceptre honestly, hold it thus: Let the thing thou sellest be a real thing, doing a real service to a real man, and let thy Persuasion be the naming of that service in its plainest coat, not the draping of an emptiness in borrowed glories. This is not a counsel of dullness; it is a counsel of Sincerity, which, rightly used, is the most arresting weapon in any Persuader's armory,— for the world is so sated with Phantasm-selling, so wearied unto death with the sixteenth reformulated Serum of Eternal Youth, that the man who stands up in the marketplace and says a true thing plainly will, before long, be heard above all the shrieking, precisely because he is the only one not shrieking.

III.

And here is the second charge upon thee, harder than the first: that thou take up, consciously and with thy whole strength, the work of Vision-Making, since Vision-Making has in any case fallen into thy lap, whether asked for or no. Every civilization that has endured has had some Class charged, formally or informally, with telling the People what is admirable, what is to be striven for, what a good life among them looks like,— the Priest did it once, and the Bard, and after them the Schoolmaster and the Editor; and now, in this Advertising Republic of ours, it is thou, oftener than any of these, who paints the picture of the Good Life that the schoolboy and the tired clerk alike carry home with them at evening. Thou canst not now resign the office; the only question left thee is whether thou wilt fill it as a Hero fills a post assigned him by the Eternities, or as a Quack fills it, mumbling incantations over an empty till.

Fill it, then, as a Hero would. Let the Republic's advertised Vision of itself be a Vision of Work well done, of the Craftsman honored above the mere Possessor, of Strength that serves rather than Strength that merely glitters; let it show forth Industry, Family, Neighbor-hood, the plain dignities that do not date and do not disappoint, rather than the eternal parade of Idleness-as-Paradise which is the laziest lie any Persuader ever told, and the most corrosive, since it teaches thirty millions of grown men and women, hour upon hour, that the highest good attainable is to want, acquire, and want again, forever, on a wheel that goes nowhere. A Nation schooled daily in that catechism will not, in the end, be a Nation of Workmen; it will be a Nation of Debtors, restless, dissatisfied, and secretly ashamed, not knowing quite why.

IV.

I hear the Advertising Man protest,— for he always protests, being by trade a most fluent creature,— that he is a Servant only, that he sells what the Client bids him sell, and Vision is none of his business, his business being Conversion and Reach and the season's numbers. To which I answer as I have answered every Stump-Orator and Phantasm-Captain of my acquaintance: that the plea of mere Servant has never yet excused a man who held, in his two hands, an instrument of such reach into thirty million souls a day. The Turnkey who merely turns the key is still the man who locked the door. Thou wast not compelled into this trade at the sword's point; thou enteredst it, and enteredst it, moreover, at the very hour it swelled from a Trade into something perilously resembling a Priesthood; and Priesthood, once assumed, however sideways, however by accident of History and Technology together, carries with it a Priest's account to render.

Render it, then, honestly. Ask, before the campaign is loosed upon the Republic, not only "Will this sell?" but the older and sterner question, "Is this a true thing I am telling my Countrymen, and will the telling of it, multiplied by thirty million repetitions, leave them a better or a worse People than it found them?" I do not say this question has an easy answer; few questions worth asking do. But I do say that the Advertising Man who never once puts it to himself, who lets his whole enormous Instrument run on the single rail of this Quarter's Numbers, is doing to his Country something not unlike what the Stump-Orator does to his Parliament,— filling the air with a great plausible Noise, out of which, examined afterward, no Fact, no Nourishment, no Cosmos was ever built, only a great emptying of the listener's own capacity to want anything real.

V.

And so, to close: America has chosen,— not by vote, not by any Act of Congress, but by the plain drift of where her money and her hours now go,— to let her vision of herself be painted chiefly by her Persuaders. This is done; it will not now be undone; the printing-press did not go back into its box once invented, nor will this. The only door left open is the door of what sort of Painters they shall be. Let them be Hucksters merely, and the picture on the wall will be a garish, flattering, forgettable thing, and the Nation that lives beneath it will grow, slowly and without quite noticing, garish and flattering and forgettable itself. Or let them remember,— some remnant of them, in agency and platform and boardroom alike,— that they hold, by History's strange and unaudited bequest, something of the old Bard's office and something of the old Priest's, and that Sincerity, not Cleverness, is the only material out of which a durable Vision was ever built for any People, in any Age; and then the picture on the wall may yet be a picture worth the having, and the Nation beneath it may yet grow toward what it is shown, rather than merely toward what it is sold.

The choice, be it never so buried under Impression-counts and Attribution-models, remains what it has always been, in every Age that ever mistook its Trade for its Destiny: Sham, or Reality. Choose.
